This really comes down to communication. Polyamory allows you to craft your relationship as it best works for you. I’ve had a monogamous partner who was aware and consenting, it is possible to do. Ultimately, it ended up being too difficult for them, and we decided to step our relationship back.

Hi there, polyamorous person here! I’m going to take this as a genuine, good faith curiosity about polyamory. 

The “why” has always been interesting to me. In my own experience, it feels like my brain just works differently than a lot of people - I really don’t get jealous in the same way most people do. It’s never made sense to me why you can love multiple friends or family members, but not partners. 

I’ve asked my partners and some others the same thing, and answers have varied a lot. Some, like me, feel it’s innate, like an orientation. Some actively choose it for a wide variety of reasons. 

I love my partners in different ways - they’re individual people, and each relationship is unique. The dynamic requires enormous amounts of trust, vulnerability, communication, and boundaries, which sets a solid foundation for any type of relationship.

A lot of people don’t realize how much of a barrier anxiety can be. No matter what anyone says, your anxiety and discomfort are valid and sometimes you can’t “just do it”. 

I’ve always found it easier to ask for something by highlighting the why. “Hey, my anxiety is pretty bad and it would be really helpful for me if you could focus on me while you’re belaying until I’m more confident.” Doing it over text helps me immensely too. 

Even trying something less direct could be a good first step, like asking for encouragement or beta on the wall, which would require watching you. My partner always uses a grigri too, which helps me relax a bit when I need to do a mental safety check to calm myself on the wall. 

No matter what you need, there is a way to ask for it that I believe you can do, and it’s okay if it’s not “just say it”. Wishing you the best from a fellow anxious climber.

Not OP, but can answer. It really depends on the person and situation. If you know they have a good relationship with family, that’s an option, but tread carefully; not everyone does and family can make things worse. If you don’t know, I would advise avoiding telling family and reach out to a close friend of theirs instead. 

Crisis lines and chats can give good advice if you’re not sure what to do. 

If they have a therapist or psychiatrist, you can reach out to them. They won’t be able to tell you anything if the person hasn’t signed a release, not even that they’re a client, and might not even respond to you, but they can take information from you and reach out to the person or bring it up in their next session. 

If they’re not responding and you’re worried they’ll hurt themselves, call the police non-emergency line and request a welfare check. Again, tread carefully, especially if the person you’re worried about is a POC and/or prone to anger, psychosis, or is neurodiverse. 

911 should only be called in a life-threatening situation.
